26.0.s.en: (1) Saul goes out to pursue David

26.0.0.en: Once again the people of Ziph volunteered to go out and inform Saul of David's new hiding place. They had informed him before in (ch. 23:19) when he pursued David, but he left him because of the Philistines' attack on the land. And the second time, at En Gedi (ch. 24:1), it was probably the Ziphites who informed him, when he entered the cave in which David was. The Ziphites, of course, wanted to gain some benefit from this in one way or another, so they went to Saul's residence at Gibeah and told him that they were certain David was in a region called "the hill of Hachilah," which is mentioned in (ch. 23:19).

26.1.0.en: Immediately Saul gathered three thousand men of Israel, chosen for their skill in war, and went out with this small army to look for David in the wilderness of Ziph, at "the hill of Hachilah."

26.2.0.en: Saul encamped with his army on "the hill of Hachilah," while David was hiding in caves inside the mountain in the wilderness opposite the hill of Hachilah. Of course David heard the commotion of Saul and his men and learned that he had come out after him.

26.3.0.en: Trench: a protective barrier for defense.

26.3.1.en: To be more certain, David sent out spies, and when they returned he knew for sure that Saul had come out to kill him. So David himself went out stealthily, and from a hidden place he looked at the site where Saul and his men were gathered, and he saw Saul himself, with Abner, the commander of his army, relaxing behind a trench for protection.

26.3.2.en: Saul was still pursuing David and had not learned from David's earlier forbearance toward him, nor from God's deliverance of him out of his hand. Do not be persistent in evil; rather repent, and do not go on in evil, lest God abandon you and allow you to be disciplined, and you suffer greatly.

26.4.s.en: (2) David goes down to Saul's place

26.4.0.en: Zeruiah: she was David's sister by his mother, and Abishai and Joab were her sons.

26.4.1.en: David spoke with Ahimelech the Hittite and with Abishai the brother of Joab, and asked the two of them, "Who will go down with me to the place where Saul is?" And Abishai answered that he would go down with him.

26.5.0.en: David crept down by night to Saul and the people gathered around him. It appears that Saul was fast asleep, he and those with him, including Abner, the commander of his army, who was primarily charged with guarding Saul. Saul's spear was stuck in the ground by his head. God allowed this deep sleep in order to show David's forbearance, as we shall see. And we see here how Saul relied on his own strength and on his strong protection in the hand of the great military commander Abner and the armies around him, and forgot that protection and strength are from God, so God showed his weakness before David.

26.6.0.en: Delivered your enemy: that is, He has given him into your hand.

26.6.1.en: It was never expected that the matter would be so easy, and so Abishai dared to speak to David, saying: The Lord has delivered Saul into your hand this day so that you may take vengeance on him; so let me strike him with his spear once, a single piercing blow that will kill him and end the days of his pursuit of you. But the forbearing David answered him with a refusal, explaining that Saul was still the king whom God had anointed, so how could he kill the one whom God had chosen, and if he did this, could he escape the wrath of God?

26.7.0.en: David was confident of God's justice and that He does not tolerate the wrong done to His children for long, so he declared that God would intervene in His own way and take vengeance on him: either he would perish in one of the wars, or God would cause him to die in His own way.

26.8.0.en: David repeated his words, that he could not stretch out his hand against Saul, the Lord's anointed, but he asked Abishai to take Saul's spear from beside him, and also the water jug set aside for his drinking. They indeed took the spear and the jug, and no one noticed them, for by divine providence a deep sleep had fallen on everyone. And David and Abishai returned to their first place.

26.8.1.en: Rise above taking your right into your own hand, and lift your grievance up to God, and trust that He hears the cry of the wronged and feels for him, for He is the hope of him who has no hope and the helper of him who has no helper. In this way you keep your peace and your love for others, and your faith increases in God, who seeks the salvation of all and disciplines them in the fitting way that leads them to repentance.

26.9.0.en: David withdrew and crossed over, returning to his first place, and went up to the top of a hill. The distance was great enough that no one could throw a dart at him, and at the same time his voice would be heard and he would be easy to see, since he was standing in a high place.

26.10.0.en: David called out in a loud voice more than once to the people and to Abner, asking him to answer and respond to him. And Abner answered, inquiring about the voice that was calling. Perhaps Abner's question carried a note of astonishment and displeasure at this call: who dares to call out to the king? It seems that Abner did not answer quickly, since he was deep in sleep and did not expect anyone to call to the king and the commander of his army.

26.11.0.en: David addressed Abner, and began his words with a question followed by a rebuke. He said to him: Are you not supposed to be the bravest of the men of Israel, and is there not a man like you in courage who can be entrusted with the king's life and guarding? Why then were you negligent and overcome by sleep, and did not do your duty? For a man came by night to kill the king, and you knew nothing of it. How then can you be a faithful servant over the life of your lord?

26.12.0.en: You have done evil, Abner, by this carelessness and unfaithfulness toward your lord the king. You and those with you who guard the king deserve death for this negligence and for not keeping safe your lord and king, Saul, the Lord's anointed. For the spear and the water jug were taken, and you did not stir to protect the king.

26.12.1.en: Be faithful in your responsibilities, whether guarding or any work that you do, so that you complete it with faithfulness and precision for the sake of God and not of men, and God will reward you for your faithfulness, in addition to which people will be pleased by it.

26.13.0.en: Saul recognized David's voice and wanted to be sure of it, so he asked him again about his voice. Saul's words were in a fatherly tone, even though he was wicked and was trying to kill David. And David answered that it was indeed he.

26.14.0.en: David continued his speech, asking: Why, O king, have you come out after me seeking my death? What evil have I done, and what crime have I committed, that you should decide my death?

26.15.0.en: Let Him accept an offering: that is, may God accept the offering.

26.15.1.en: David began to present his case to King Saul with humility, describing himself as a servant appealing to his master, and he said to him: If it is God who has sent you out after me because of some fault I may have committed, then tell me and give me time to offer a sacrifice for my sin to God, perhaps He will accept it and forgive me. But if it is men who have slandered me to you without any real offense, then let them be cursed before the Lord, for by doing this it is as though they have driven me out from before the Lord and His worship, so that I should take refuge with other people who serve other gods.

26.15.2.en: Note David's courtesy in speaking with Saul. Although he knew Saul's evil and his hatred toward him, he attributed the evil to others who were speaking evil about him to Saul, in order to give Saul an opportunity to turn back from his evil.

26.16.0.en: Partridge: a mountain bird that hunters chased in order to eat it; when it grew tired of flying it would come down to the ground and be easy to catch.

26.16.1.en: David used here a manner of forbidding, the meaning of which is that it is unthinkable for the king to shed his blood before God, because he is innocent and his blood would cry out from the ground like the blood of Abel. He continued, expressing his amazement at how the great king of Israel could come out after a weak servant of his servants. He applied to himself the title of the flea as a way of belittling himself, and he also described himself as that mountain bird which hunters chase, yet which has no worth or price.

26.16.2.en: David's excellence in this dialogue with Saul appears in the following:

26.16.3.en: 1- His humility, and his describing himself as a flea or a partridge.

26.16.4.en: 2- His confidence in himself, as he boldly declares that he is innocent.

26.16.5.en: 3- His courtesy, as he attaches the evil to others who incited Saul to it, in order to give him a chance to turn back.

26.16.6.en: 4- His readiness to declare his apology for any fault he had done, and to offer repentance and a sacrifice.

26.16.7.en: 5- His attachment and longing for communal worship with his people in the house of the Lord.

26.17.0.en: By the work of divine grace Saul was moved by David's words and quickly reconsidered. He began his apology by acknowledging his error in going out after David, and promised him not to harm him, especially as David had preserved his life and had not killed him. With remorse he also acknowledged his foolishness and error and that he had lost his reason, and he asked David to return from his flight to his home and his clan in safety.

26.17.1.en: Apologizing with humility when one is at fault is a beautiful virtue adorning the true Christian, so do not let your pride stand in the way of your apology when you are at fault.

26.18.0.en: David did not trust Saul completely, for he had previously promised David safety and then broken his covenant. So David did not come down to give Saul his spear, but asked one of Saul's men to come over and approach David to take the king's spear.

26.19.0.en: David prayed that the Lord would give and reward everyone according to his righteousness and faithfulness. Of course he is referring here to himself, and he also points out that he had been faithful toward Saul, since when the opportunity was given him to kill him he did not do so.

26.20.0.en: And as David did with Saul, David asks and prays that he too might find grace in the eyes of God, and that He would deliver him from his enemies or from every tribulation to which he might be exposed.

26.20.1.en: And David here puts his trust in God, who does not go back on His promises and protects His children, whereas men like Saul are, sadly, not dependable in their promises.

26.21.0.en: This chapter ends contrary to how it began, and the picture changes completely, for Saul prays a blessing for David, whereas at the beginning of the chapter he blessed the Ziphites, David's enemies, who were trying to deliver him up to him. The expression "you shall both do great things and also still prevail" is meant to say that you may always be able to pardon and forgive. And both departed: Saul returned to his city, and David went on his way.

27.0.s.en: (1) David takes refuge with Achish, king of Gath

27.0.0.en: With Saul's repeated attempts to kill David and his continual pursuit, David did not trust his promises, which he had given before and then broken. So for the second time David thought that there was no escape for him except to flee to Gath, one of the great cities of the Philistines. He had fled to Gath the first time, and the king's men tried to stir the king up against David, so he feigned madness and the king let him go (ch. 21:10-15). By this he would avoid Saul's pursuit, since Saul would not think of waging war with the Philistines for David's sake. And indeed he took his six hundred men with him and crossed the border to "Achish," king of "Gath."

27.0.1.en: The men following him numbered 600, in addition to their wives and children, a large number, and perhaps David felt that it was hard for their life in the caves and hideouts to continue, so he thought of taking refuge in a city of the Philistines.

27.0.2.en: And perhaps David did not consult God before going to Gath because he was forced to use cunning so that the king of Gath would not rise up against him, and God, for the sake of his righteousness throughout his life, kept him safe with the king of Gath and delivered him from embarrassing situations, as we shall see in the following chapters.

27.0.3.en: It appears to us that it would have been better for David to remain pursued by Saul in the land of Judah, relying on God's promise to keep him and make him king, rather than taking refuge with the idolaters, especially since God's voice to him through the mouth of Gad the prophet had been, "Abide not in the hold; depart, and get thee into the land of Judah" (ch. 22:5), meaning that God was able to keep him while he was a pursued stranger in the land of Judah.

27.1.0.en: Achish allowed David to dwell in "Gath" with his two wives, "Ahinoam" and "Abigail," and all his men as well. Perhaps Achish, the king of the Philistines, considered David and his men a force not to be taken lightly, one that would add great strength to his army, and because he knew of the enmity between David and Saul, he regarded David as an ally who would help him against Saul.

27.2.0.en: Saul learned of "David's" flight to Gath and his settling there, so he gave up on him and did not go out to pursue him afterward, for fear of the Philistines.

27.3.0.en: David did not want to stay long in "Gath," since it was the capital of the king and he and his men would always be under watch there, and for fear of slanders or problems that his men might cause. So he preferred to leave for somewhere farther away so that he might have a greater measure of freedom that would allow him to worship God with his men, because his being in Gath might expose him to pressure from its king to burn incense to the idols with the rest of his royal court. In addition, if he succeeded and grew strong and his men increased, or if he won victories in any raids, the king of Gath might become afraid of him through the slander of some of his royal court. So he came forward and asked the king to give him a place in one of the villages.

27.4.0.en: Ziklag: it lies ten miles north of Beersheba.

27.4.1.en: The Lord gave David favor in the eyes of King Achish, so he granted his request and gave him the village of "Ziklag," which lies on the border. It had originally been part of the land of Judah, and the Philistines seized it in one of the wars, and it remained in their hands throughout Saul's life; afterward the kings of Judah recovered it and it became part of their lands and kingdoms. The inspired text tells us the period that David spent in this town: it was a year and four months.

27.4.2.en: God gave David favor in the eyes of King Achish, so that he did not suspect him and received him as his guest. So trust that if you please God and keep His commandments, He will give you favor in the eyes of all, even your enemies, so that they live at peace with you and you grow in your relationship with God without hindrance.

27.5.0.en: During David's stay in Gath he raided some of the pagan tribes, whose life was largely of a nomadic character. These tribes and their small lands were spread out from the borders of Shur, which is south of Palestine, to the east of Egypt. The most important of these peoples were the Geshurites, the Gezrites, and the Amalekites, peoples whom God commanded to be fought, all of them.

27.6.0.en: David's wars and raids were comprehensive: he destroyed all the inhabitants of these places and was able to take their spoil of sheep, cattle, donkeys, and camels, besides the fabrics and garments. Perhaps the purpose of these raids of David was:

27.6.1.en: 1- To destroy the pagan peoples dwelling on the southern border of the tribe of Judah, thus securing the land of that tribe, to which he belonged.

27.6.2.en: 2- To obtain spoil sufficient for the needs of his men for their livelihood.

27.6.3.en: 3- To make Achish believe that he had attacked the Jews, so that he would become loyal and subject to him, as will appear in (v. 10).

27.7.0.en: Whither have ye made a road today: an interrogative expression whose meaning is "whom have you raided today," as it appears in the Septuagint.

27.7.1.en: "Achish" asked David about the peoples he had raided, and David answered cunningly, with an answer that had more than one meaning. David answered him that he had raided the south of Judah and the south of the Jerahmeelites, who are Jewish peoples, and also the south of the Kenites, friends of the Jews, from whom came Jethro, the father-in-law of Moses, and Heber the Kenite, the husband of Jael, who killed Sisera (Judg 4). David's answer suggested that he had raided the southern outskirts of these peoples, but he had not done this; rather he raided the peoples who lie south of these regions, and by this cunning he wanted to suggest to Achish that he had raided the Jewish peoples themselves, and so become an enemy of the Jews and a vassal of the Philistines. David's raiding of the lands neighboring the tribe of Judah was a common practice at this time, as a securing of the borders of the land by seizing the lands adjacent to them.

27.8.0.en: This verse comes on its own as an explanation for David's killing everyone he raided, so that none of these peoples would come and report to Achish that David had used the land of the Philistines as a base from which to kill these pagan tribes and not the Jews, as he had led Achish to believe.

27.9.0.en: David's trick worked on Achish, who believed that he had raided his own people and rejoiced greatly at this. He thought that by this deed David had become hated by his people Israel, many of whom he had killed, and that he would therefore become a mighty servant of strength, subject to him, whom Achish could use in wars.

27.9.1.en: God is able to give you strength however hard your circumstances may be, like David's being with the Philistines, his enemies, and his victory in his raids and the provision of his men's needs. So do not worry, for God arranges your needs and opens ways for you to live and rejoice with Him.

27.9.2.en: Saul's consulting the medium before the war
